attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his Substack post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Faithful restatement of a present-state adoption claim. There are no conditions or horizon to preserve.

contract.note: Plain reading of 'large fraction' as a substantial minority, measured in US adults, is an ordinary reading that favours neither side. Counting health information-seeking as medical advice is a reasonable reading of the speaker's words.

evidence.note: KFF nationally representative survey of US adults, fieldwork Feb 24–Mar 2 2026, published before the post. About 32% had used chatbots for health information in the past year, and 13% had uploaded medical data for advice.

reviews.rationale: An independent representative survey available before the post found about one in three US adults intentionally using AI chatbots for health information or advice. That meets the contract's substantial-minority reading. The packet has no contrary representative data. Limits: US adults only, and the measure is health information broadly rather than advice narrowly.

attribution.note: The parenthetical is Marcus's own assertion within his recommendation sentence.

semantics.note: The causal parenthetical is correctly separated from the surrounding normative advice not to trust LLMs with our lives.

contract.note: Reading 'illusion' as misleading, overstated certainty, with training as a contributing cause, is an ordinary plain reading. A stricter reading (confidence wholly meaningless, training as the sole cause) would be harder to support.

evidence.note: ICLR 2025 paper, available before the post. RLHF models show more verbalized overconfidence than pre-RLHF models, reward models favour high confidence regardless of quality, and calibrated reward training reduces calibration error.

EMNLP 2023. RLHF worsens token-probability calibration, but elicited verbal confidence can be fairly well calibrated in some models. This limits an absolute reading but does not refute the contributing-cause reading.

June 2026 preprint, before the evaluation date. Across six open-weight models, instruction tuning harms calibration and the chat format adds overconfidence. Supports training as one cause among others.

reviews.rationale: Controlled before-and-after and reward-intervention experiments (e1, e3) show that post-training raises expressed confidence beyond what correctness warrants. That meets the support condition. e2 shows confidence is not wholly uninformative, which the contract says limits only a universal reading. Proprietary medical chatbots were not tested directly.
